name: Olga Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Olga. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. Could you start by telling me a little about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Olga, I'm 27, and I'm a junior lawyer at Quayside Law, a small firm in a port town. We advise the businesses around the harbour: fishing boat owners, a ship repair yard, haulage firms, mostly on contracts and the rules they have to follow. My partner Daniel is a ship's engineer, so he's away at sea for six weeks at a time, and I keep the flat and the cat going on my own.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm usually in by eight. I use AI every day: I feed it the new fishing rules and get it to sort out what changed for each client, then I check it and write a short letter. I also get it to do a first pass on contracts, which I then mark up. I'm not the strongest on the law yet, I still miss things the partner, Mrs Okoye, catches, but I'm quick and the clients like that I answer on the same day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's a handy tool, and the market sorted out the hype. Businesses that use it well get a small edge, and that's how it should be. I'd probably post something like that on the harbour business group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my edge stays small and so does my pay. I've got less than a month of savings, and the flat costs more since the landlord put the rent up in September. There are only two firms in town that do this work, so I can't easily move for more money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI to answer clients faster than anyone else, and ask Mrs Okoye to let me take a few small clients of my own. I'd start saving properly, a hundred a month, once Daniel's next contract pays. And I'd start planning a small practice of my own, maybe in three or four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit restless. It's not frightening, it's just slow. I like a bit more going on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your own practice? With thin savings, how?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's why it's three or four years away. With AI doing the drafting, a one-woman firm for the harbour businesses could run from a room above the chandlery. I'd want enough saved to cover six months first, because I'm not daft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Daniel's work shape all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When Daniel (her partner) is at sea, I'm on my own with every bill, so I'm careful. His pay is good but it comes in lumps. I've learned to budget like a fishing family, for the bad months as well as the good.

say: AI is a **handy tool**, and the **market** sorted out the hype.
Businesses that use it well get a **small edge**, which is how it should be.
think: My edge stays small and so does my **pay**.
With rent up and only **two firms** in town, I can't easily move for money.
do: Ask Mrs Okoye for a few **small clients** of her own.
Save **a hundred a month** once Daniel's next contract pays.
Plan a **one-woman practice** in three or four years.
S0.quote: I've learned to budget like a fishing family, for the bad months as well as the good.
fieldNote: She's **adaptive** and slightly **bored** by a slow-change world.
Her free-market view shows in her plan to **start her own** practice.
Daniel's **lumpy pay** and her thin cushion make her careful, not frightened.

steps.text: Ask Mrs Okoye to hand her a few small harbour clients
Save a hundred a month once Daniel's contract pays
Plan a one-woman harbour law practice above the chandlery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is an opportunity for people willing to work and adapt. I wouldn't be asking the government for anything, I'd be telling businesses to get on with it. On the harbour group I'd offer to show people what I use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm in a decent position, because I already do this every day. The firm will need fewer juniors, but the one who runs the tools and keeps clients happy has a better chance. I'm a bit worried for my friend Lewis at the other firm, who refuses to touch any of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd pitch Mrs Okoye a fixed-fee rules-checking service for the fishing boats, run mostly by AI and checked by me. If she said no, I'd start it myself on the side. I'd also keep saving, because a new business needs a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared. It feels like the tide coming in and I've got a boat. The worry is that I'm still not as good at the law as I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to people like Lewis?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Lewis (her friend at the other firm) will have a hard few years unless he changes. I'd try to talk him round over a pint. But I'm not going to pretend the world owes him the old way of doing things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not as good at the law as you'd like. Does that worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit. If the machine does the drafting, the human needs to be the one who knows when it's wrong. I'd do the extra courses on fishing rules at night, because that's where I'm weakest.

I'd tell businesses to **get on with it**, not wait for the government.

steps.text: Pitch Mrs Okoye a fixed-fee rules-checking service for fishing boats

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but people and businesses will find new ways to earn, like they always have. I'd say families need to stick together and help each other through. I wouldn't be calling for handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my legal job is gone by 2029, and so is my clever little service, because AI won't need me to check it. That stings. Daniel's work is hands-on, fixing engines at sea, so he has until about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd sit down with Daniel and plan around his wage, because it lasts longer than mine. I'd use the two years to build a business that needs a person on the dock, maybe inspecting boats before a sale, using AI for the paperwork. I'd cut everything else and save every pound I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's frightening, but I'm the type who feels better once I'm doing something. I'd keep busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why boat inspections?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone has to climb down into the engine room and look. I grew up around the harbour, my dad sold boats, I know what rust and bodges look like. Robots will get there, but probably not till 2031, and a dock is a messy place for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would tell me to stop moaning and get working, and he'd be right. He's never had a pension or a boss. I'd go to him for contacts in the boat trade.

say: It's a **shock**, but people will find **new ways** to earn.
Families should **stick together** rather than call for **handouts**.
think: My legal job and my **checking service** are likely gone by **2029**.
Daniel's hands-on **engine work** lasts until about **2031**.
do: Build a **boat inspection** business that needs someone on the dock.
S2.quote: Someone has to climb down into the engine room and look.
fieldNote: She uses the **robot gap** to move toward hands-on **boat inspections**.
She leans on **family**, Daniel's wage and her dad's contacts, not state help.
Losing her **AI service** to AI itself stings her the most.

steps.text: Plan the household budget around Daniel's ship engineer wage
Start a boat inspection business using her dad's contacts
Cut all spending except rent and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent warning, and anyone who wastes it can't complain. I'd be telling people at the harbour to start something now. I'd put it plainly, maybe too plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd get three or four good years out of my legal work, maybe even my own practice. After 2031 the thinking side's gone. So I'd use the time to build something hands-on alongside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my rules-checking service for the fishing boats in the first year, using AI to keep costs low. I'd put the profit into a boat surveyor's course, so I'm qualified by 2029. And I'd keep three months of savings, which would be a first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. Five years feels like enough to make two careers work. I'd be tired, but I'd sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Daniel change any plans, like marriage or children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably marry in the next couple of years, small, at the harbour chapel. Children later, once the surveying is earning. I'm not someone who waits forever, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your service did well and you made money from AI. Would that change your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, that's just how markets work. You do something useful, you get paid. If AI makes my service redundant in 2031, then I move again.

S3.quote: You do something useful, you get paid. If AI makes my service redundant in 2031, then I move again.
fieldNote: She plans **two careers** at once: an AI service and boat surveying.

steps.text: Launch the AI rules-checking service for fishing boats

Build three months of savings for the first time
Marry Daniel at the harbour chapel in the next two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone with a bit of get-up-and-go. I'd be telling young people to learn a practical skill as well as a profession. I'd post about my plans, because that's how you find customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I could have a proper legal business for most of the decade, and do well. The risk is too much confidence. But I've got time to build a hands-on skill before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd open my own harbour law practice within three years, run lean with AI. I'd take the boat surveyor's course part-time around 2030. And I'd buy a small flat with Daniel once the practice is earning, near the harbour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than not. Ten years is a long time to build things. I'd feel almost lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a flat when your profession has an end date. Is that wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying a flat is a risk, but bricks don't get automated. Daniel's wage lasts longer than mine, and a flat near the harbour always rents out. I'd rather own something than rent forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger lawyer starting out now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the tools, learn the law, and learn something you can do with your hands. Have three legs to stand on. I'd say it to anyone, not just lawyers.

say: **Ten years** is a gift for anyone with **get-up-and-go**.
Young people should learn a **practical skill** as well as a profession.
think: I could run a proper **legal business** for most of the decade.
My risk is **too much confidence**, but there's time for a **hands-on** skill.

S4.quote: Buying a flat is a risk, but bricks don't get automated.
fieldNote: With a decade she sees **opportunity** more than threat.
She'd **invest in property** as a hedge against her own job ending.

steps.text: Open her own harbour law practice within three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's the one where my service and my job go before I've built anything else. What would help is fewer rules stopping people starting small businesses, and cheap short courses in practical trades.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who are excited. Everyone assumes young lawyers are terrified. I'm a bit scared, but I'm also itching to build something of my own.

headlineQuote: I'm a bit scared, but I'm also itching to build something of my own.
portrait: Olga is a **27-year-old** junior at a **small port-town** firm advising harbour businesses.
She uses **AI daily** and wants her own **one-woman practice**.
Her partner Daniel is a **ship's engineer** away at sea, and their savings are thin.
She sees **opportunity** first and leans on family and markets, not government.
In every AGI picture she moves toward **hands-on boat work**, inspecting and surveying.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing her job and service before **building** anything else.
whatWouldHelp: **Fewer rules** for small businesses and cheap short **trade courses**.
